NO. 041 · Coast & Tidal Flats / Scolopacidae · Sandpipers & Snipes

Common Sandpiper

矶鹬 · jī yù Actitis hypoleucos
Winter visitor Common 18–21 cm Protected (China) IUCN LC

The sandpiper that trots along the waterline, tail bobbing

It does not gather on the big mudflats. It works alone along a riverbank or reservoir edge at a trot — a few steps and a stop, tail pumping up and down, wings flicked out and folded again. That routine is the Common Sandpiper's signature.

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • Wing bendA distinct white wedge at the shoulder, running forward as a white 'shoulder strap' — visible even when perched.
  • BreastGrey-brown patches at the sides of the breast running up the sides of the neck, meeting the white belly along an irregular line.
  • BillMedium length, dead straight, pale at the base and dark at the tip.
  • BehaviourBobs its tail continuously when perched, with a quick flick of the wings that is then folded away — almost impossible to misidentify.

Behaviour

Usually alone or in pairs, distributed linearly along the waterline, rarely gathering in the big flocks of other waders. It walks in stops and starts, pecking at waterside insects and small invertebrates. When flushed it flies low over the surface with stiff, downward-pressed wingbeats. A winter visitor in South China, commonest along rivers and reservoir edges.

Voice

Recording Joost van Bruggen · Licence CC BY-SA 4.0 · Original file

A very loud three-note whistle, 'swee-wee-wee', the first note high and the last two slightly lower, given almost invariably on take-off — the main way to find the bird.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • Qianshan River banks
  • Qianwu Reservoir shores
  • Xiangshan Lake Park waterfront
  • Doumen tidal creeks
Field note
Hear that sharp 'swee-wee-wee'? Follow the waterline to the lone bird trotting along with its tail pumping — that is the Common Sandpiper.
